title: NFC Supplier for Japan — Tags, Cards & Inlays
summary: Proud Tek supplies NFC and UHF RFID to Japan factory-direct from Shenzhen with Japanese-market spec sheets. Japan runs contactless on two tracks: HF at 13.56 MHz — where our NFC Forum NTAG and MIFARE products sit alongside the FeliCa infrastructure behind Suica and Osaifu-Keitai — and UHF in the 920 MHz band for retail and logistics. The one fact that decides a UHF order: Japan's RAIN band is 916.7-920.9 MHz (high-power, up to 1 W / 4 W EIRP) under MIC's Radio Act and ARIB STD-T106, so inlays are tuned for the 920 MHz band — EU 865-868 MHz stock reads short. Express air reaches Tokyo, Osaka and Nagoya in 3-5 business days; RFID proximity cards and tags enter at 0% import duty (HS 8523.52) with 10% consumption tax, and DDP is available.

sections.title: Get the band right: Japan's 920 MHz band under MIC and ARIB
sections.intro: The single most expensive mistake in cross-border RFID sourcing is band mismatch. Japan's UHF RAIN band lives in the 920 MHz band — 916.7-920.9 MHz for high-power (up to 1 W / 4 W EIRP) readers under MIC's Radio Act and ARIB STD-T106, and 916.7-923.5 MHz for specified-low-power (250 mW) devices under ARIB STD-T107. It sits inside the upper part of the US 902-928 MHz allocation but nowhere near the EU 865-868 MHz band, so EU-tuned inlays read short. Order 920 MHz-band tuning on the PO, and see our [LF vs HF vs UHF guide](/blog/rfid-frequencies-lf-hf-uhf-explained/) or [RAIN RFID explainer](/guides/rain-rfid-explained/) if you are new to frequency planning.

sections.title: Landed cost: HS 8523.52, 0% duty and 10% consumption tax
sections.intro: The unit price is the headline; the landed cost is the story. For Japan the plot is short — the HS line is duty-free and the tax is a flat 10%. Our [RFID RFP template](/blog/rfid-rfp-template-questions-suppliers/) shows the quote-comparison math in full; the short version is below.

dataHighlight.heading: RFID proximity cards and tags enter Japan duty-free; the live line is the 10% consumption tax
dataHighlight.text: Japan's tariff schedule lists RFID under HS 8523.52.010 ("Proximity cards and tags") at a Free — 0% — general duty rate, because smart cards are covered by the WTO Information Technology Agreement. That zero applies regardless of origin, so RCEP (in force between China and Japan) adds nothing on this line — there is no tariff to eliminate. What remains is the 10% Japan Consumption Tax, charged at import on the customs value plus any duty. On a DDP quote, freight, consumption tax and clearance are folded into one price; confirm the classification with your customs broker.

faq.question: Which UHF band do your tags use for Japan?
faq.answer: Japan's UHF RAIN band is the 920 MHz band: 916.7-920.9 MHz for high-power readers (up to 1 W conducted / 4 W EIRP) under ARIB STD-T106, and 916.7-923.5 MHz for specified-low-power (250 mW) devices under ARIB STD-T107, both regulated by MIC under the Radio Act. We tune passive inlays for the 920 MHz band. EU 865-868 MHz inlays read short on a Japanese portal and are not a drop-in. HF NFC and access cards at 13.56 MHz are global and unaffected — specify 920 MHz-band tuning only for UHF inlay and label orders.

faq.question: Do your NFC products work with Japanese smartphones and alongside FeliCa?
faq.answer: Yes. Japanese iPhones and most Android phones sold in Japan (Sony Xperia, Sharp Aquos, Samsung Galaxy) read both FeliCa (Type F) and NFC Forum (Type 2/4). Our NTAG-based tags comply with NFC Forum Type 2 and Type 4 and tap on any NFC-enabled Japanese smartphone. Note that we supply NFC Forum and MIFARE/ICODE products, not FeliCa chips — FeliCa is Sony's separately licensed ecosystem (Suica, Osaifu-Keitai). Our HF products coexist with it; they do not replace it.

faq.question: Do passive RFID tags need their own Giteki certification in Japan?
faq.answer: No. Under the Radio Act the type-conformity obligation — the Giteki (Technical Conformity Mark) — sits with the radio transmitter, which for RFID is the reader/interrogator. Passive UHF and NFC tags backscatter the reader's field and fall below the Radio Law's field-strength threshold, so they are exempt from mandatory Giteki certification. What matters is that the tag antenna is tuned for the 920 MHz band and the reader carries a valid Giteki number — ask your reader vendor for it, and ask us for the tag tuning data.

faq.question: How do Japanese import duty and consumption tax work on an order?
faq.answer: RFID cards and tags classify under HS 8523.52.010 ("Proximity cards and tags"), which Japan's tariff schedule lists at a Free — 0% — duty rate because smart cards are covered by the WTO Information Technology Agreement. So there is no import tariff regardless of origin, and RCEP adds nothing on this line. The remaining cost is the 10% Japan Consumption Tax on the customs value at import, generally creditable for a registered business. On a DDP quote, freight, consumption tax and clearance are included in the price up front — confirm the classification with your customs broker.

faq.question: What is the total delivery time to Japan including production?
faq.answer: Japan is one of our fastest destinations. Express air freight from Shenzhen to Tokyo, Osaka or Nagoya takes 3-5 business days; with standard production of 5-7 business days, most orders arrive within 8-12 days of confirmation. Bulk programmes on sea freight take longer and are planned against a blanket agreement.

faq.question: What is the minimum order quantity for Japanese buyers?
faq.answer: MOQ depends on the product and personalisation and is quoted per order with your target tag or card, artwork and annual volume. Free samples for compatibility and quality testing are available before any commitment — request them with your reader model and use-case.
